Graduate Thesis Formatting Guidelines 2025

Issued by: Graduate Office  
Effective: January 2025

These guidelines outline the formatting requirements for submitting master’s theses at the university. Adherence to these standards is mandatory for thesis acceptance. If you have questions, please contact the Graduate Office.

1. General Requirements

1.1 Submission Format  
Theses must be submitted as a single PDF document, with all pages included in one file. Ensure the file is readable and free of password protection.

1.2 Language  
All theses must be written in English unless prior approval has been granted by the Graduate Office.

1.3 Length  
While length varies by discipline, most master’s theses are between 60–120 pages, including all front matter and appendices.

2. Page Layout

2.1 Paper Size  
Use standard US Letter (8.5" x 11") or A4 (210mm x 297mm) size.

2.2 Margins  
Set margins as follows:  
- Left margin: 1.5 inches (to allow for binding)  
- Right margin: 1 inch  
- Top margin: 1 inch  
- Bottom margin: 1 inch

All page numbers, headers, and footers must fall within these margins.

2.3 Pagination  
Number all pages consecutively except for the title page (which is counted but not numbered). Use Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3…) beginning with the first page of the main text.

Front matter (abstract, acknowledgments, table of contents) should use lowercase Roman numerals (i, ii, iii…). The numbering begins on the abstract page.

Page numbers should appear at the bottom center or bottom right corner of each page, at least 0.5 inches from the edge.

3. Font and Spacing

3.1 Typeface  
Use a standard serif font such as Times New Roman or Garamond. The font size must be 12-point throughout the document, including footnotes and endnotes.

3.2 Line Spacing  
Main text must be double-spaced. Block quotations, footnotes, captions, tables, and bibliography entries may be single-spaced.

3.3 Paragraphs  
Indent paragraphs consistently by 0.5 inches or use a blank line between paragraphs; do not use both.

4. Title Page and Front Matter

4.1 Title Page  
Include the following information centered on the page:

- Full thesis title
- Author’s name
- Degree sought (e.g., Master of Science)
- Department/Program
- University name
- Month and year of submission

Do not include page numbers on the title page.

4.2 Abstract  
The abstract must summarize research objectives, methods, results, and conclusions in no more than 350 words. Place the abstract after the title page; number this page “i” using lowercase Roman numerals.

4.3 Acknowledgments (optional)  
If included, place after the abstract and before the table of contents.

4.4 Table of Contents  
List all sections and subsections with corresponding page numbers. Include appendices and references.

4.5 List of Figures/Tables (if applicable)  
Provide separate lists for figures and tables immediately after the table of contents if your thesis includes them.

5. Main Text Structure

Organize your thesis into clearly labeled sections:

- Introduction
- Literature Review
- Methodology/Materials and Methods
- Results
- Discussion/Analysis
- Conclusion
- References/Bibliography

Include section headings that are bolded or underlined for clarity; use consistent formatting throughout.

6. Tables, Figures, and Illustrations

6.1 Placement  
Tables and figures should appear as close as possible to their first mention in the text.

6.2 Numbering and Captions  
Number tables and figures consecutively (Table 1, Table 2; Figure 1, Figure 2). Provide descriptive captions above tables and below figures in single spacing.

6.3 Size and Quality  
Ensure all images are clear and legible at print resolution (minimum 300 dpi). Avoid color schemes that do not reproduce well in grayscale unless color is necessary for comprehension.

6.4 Permissions  
Obtain written permission to reproduce copyrighted material; cite sources appropriately beneath each item as required.

7. Citations and References

7.1 Citation Style  
Follow your department’s recommended citation style (APA, MLA, Chicago/Turabian, IEEE). Consistency is mandatory throughout your document.

7.2 In-text Citations  
Cite all sources used directly in your research according to your chosen style guidelines.

7.3 Reference List/Bibliography  
Place this section at the end of your thesis but before any appendices.
Format entries according to style guidelines.
Single-space individual entries; double-space between entries.
Check that all citations in text appear in your reference list/bibliography.

8. Appendices

Appendices may include supplementary material such as data tables, survey instruments, or additional documentation.
Label each appendix alphabetically (Appendix A, Appendix B).
Start each appendix on a new page.
Include appendices in your table of contents with correct pagination.

9. Footnotes and Endnotes

Use footnotes sparingly for supplementary explanations or comments.
Number footnotes consecutively throughout each chapter.
Footnote text should be single-spaced in 10–12 point font.
Endnotes are acceptable only if required by your citation style; place endnotes at the end of each chapter or at thesis end before references/bibliography.

10. Binding and Printing Requirements

10.1 Electronic Submission  
Submit an electronic copy as a single PDF through the designated graduate portal before the posted deadline.
Check that your PDF opens correctly on multiple devices before submission.

10.2 Hard Copy Submission (if required)  
If a hard copy is required:
Print single-sided on high-quality white paper (minimum 20 lb).
Do not staple or bind yourself; official binding will be done by university services.
Include signed approval forms with hard copies when submitting to Graduate Office.
Check with your department regarding additional copies needed for supervisors or committee members.

11. Copyright Statement

Include a copyright statement on its own page immediately following the title page:
Copyright © [Year] [Your Name]. All rights reserved.
You retain copyright ownership unless otherwise stipulated by funding agreements or publishers.
If you wish to make your thesis available through open access repositories or external publishers, consult with the Graduate Office regarding procedures and permissions.

12. Ethical Compliance Statement

If your research involved human subjects, animals, or sensitive data:
Include an ethical compliance statement indicating IRB/IACUC approval number(s), if applicable.
Place this statement after acknowledgments or before methodology section as directed by your program guidelines.
Attach copies of approval letters as appendices if required by your department or supervisor.

13. Plagiarism Policy

The university strictly prohibits plagiarism in any form.
All submitted theses will be checked using plagiarism detection software.
Properly cite all sources; failure to do so may result in disciplinary action up to degree revocation.

14. Final Checklist Before Submission

Before submitting your thesis:
- Verify compliance with all formatting rules outlined here.
- Confirm that all pages are present and correctly ordered.
- Check spelling and grammar throughout.
- Ensure that all figures/tables/images are clear and properly labeled.
- Make sure citations are complete and consistent.
- Obtain signatures from committee members where required.
- Complete any departmental forms needed for graduation clearance.
Failure to meet these requirements may delay degree conferral or result in rejection of your thesis submission.

15. Contact Information

For clarification on formatting rules or assistance with submission:
Graduate Office – Thesis Administration  
Email: gradoffice@university.edu  
Phone: (555) 123-4567  

Additional resources:
Formatting templates are available upon request from the Graduate Office website.
Workshops on thesis preparation are held twice per semester—check university calendar for dates.


Thank you for adhering to these guidelines as you prepare your master’s thesis for submission.

SOCI201 Discussion Notes  
Topic: Urban Inequality  
Date: [Yesterday’s date]

Introduction  
- The discussion section focused on urban inequality, exploring its dimensions, causes, and potential solutions.
- Key readings for this session included excerpts from "Urban Fortunes" by John Logan and Harvey Molotch, and the article "The New Urban Poverty" by William Julius Wilson.

Definition of Urban Inequality  
- Urban inequality refers to disparities in resources, opportunities, living conditions, and access to services within cities.
- Manifested in differences in income, housing quality, education, healthcare access, employment opportunities, and exposure to crime and environmental hazards.

Historical Context  
- Industrialization led to rapid urban growth; cities attracted diverse populations seeking jobs.
- Segregation (both racial and economic) shaped city landscapes; policies such as redlining and restrictive covenants contributed to unequal development.
- Post-WWII suburbanization intensified urban divides—middle-class (mostly white) populations moved out of city centers, leaving behind marginalized communities.

Key Dimensions of Urban Inequality  
1. Economic Disparities  
   - Income gaps between neighborhoods; concentration of poverty in certain areas.
   - Wealth accumulation is often tied to property ownership—those excluded from homeownership face long-term disadvantages.
   - Informal economies are prevalent in poorer urban areas due to lack of formal job opportunities.

2. Housing  
   - Affordable housing shortages force low-income residents into substandard conditions or homelessness.
   - Gentrification: influx of wealthier residents drives up rents and displaces existing communities.
   - Public housing policies have sometimes concentrated poverty rather than alleviating it.

3. Education  
   - Schools in affluent neighborhoods benefit from higher property taxes, better facilities, and more experienced teachers.
   - Urban schools serving low-income communities face underfunding, overcrowding, and lower graduation rates.
   - School segregation persists due to residential patterns.

4. Healthcare Access  
   - Hospitals and clinics are unevenly distributed; some neighborhoods have limited access to care.
   - Environmental health risks (e.g., lead exposure, air pollution) disproportionately affect low-income urban areas.

5. Crime and Policing  
   - Higher crime rates often reported in impoverished urban neighborhoods; however, causes are complex (not just poverty).
   - Policing practices can exacerbate inequalities (e.g., over-policing of minority communities).

A. Causes of Urban Inequality  
- Structural Factors:
  * Economic restructuring: Decline of manufacturing jobs hit inner-city populations hardest.

  * Educational attainment affects job prospects.
  * Family background influences social mobility.

   - Historically African American neighborhood affected by redlining and disinvestment.
   - Recent gentrification in nearby areas has not benefited long-term residents.

2. Detroit’s Decline  
   - Collapse of auto industry led to mass unemployment and population loss.
   - City government struggled to provide basic services; blight became widespread.

3. New York City Public Housing  
   - NYCHA developments house hundreds of thousands but suffer from chronic underfunding.
   - Waiting lists for affordable units are years long; maintenance issues are common.

- Definition: Process where wealthier individuals move into historically lower-income neighborhoods, changing the area’s character and raising costs.

   - Empowerment zones offer tax incentives for businesses investing in distressed areas.

- What mechanisms ensure accountability when implementing anti-poverty programs?

3. “There Goes the Neighborhood” by Mari Gallagher – investigates food deserts and health outcomes in Chicago.

Conclusion

- Urban inequality is multifaceted—rooted in history but continually reshaped by policy choices and market forces.
- Solutions require coordinated efforts across government levels, community organizations, and private sector actors.
- Next week’s discussion will focus on environmental justice within urban settings—how pollution impacts different city communities unequally.

Final Project Grading Rubric  
CS320 – Data Structures and Algorithms

Overview:  
This rubric outlines the criteria by which final project reports for CS320 will be evaluated. The report is expected to demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of data structures and algorithms, their application to a real-world or theoretical problem, and the ability to communicate findings effectively. Please review each section carefully to ensure your submission meets all requirements.

Total Points: 100

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I. Problem Definition and Motivation (15 points)

Criteria:
- Clarity in describing the problem addressed (5 points)
- Justification for selecting the problem; relevance to course topics (5 points)
- Explanation of why the problem is significant or interesting (5 points)

Exceeds Expectations (13–15):
- The problem is clearly articulated with context and background.
- The motivation is compelling, showing deep engagement with course concepts.
- Importance and relevance are thoroughly explained.

Meets Expectations (10–12):
- The problem is stated with adequate clarity.
- Motivation and relevance are described but may lack depth.
- Some connection to course material is established.

Below Expectations (7–9):
- The problem statement lacks detail or clarity.
- Motivation is weak or superficial.
- Limited connection to data structures/algorithms.

Unacceptable (<7):
- Problem definition missing or unclear.
- No evident motivation or relevance.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
II. Literature Review / Related Work (10 points)

Criteria:
- Identification of relevant prior work, solutions, or approaches (5 points)
- Discussion of strengths/weaknesses of existing methods (3 points)
- Clear positioning of your project within existing literature (2 points)

Exceeds Expectations (9–10):
- Comprehensive review with multiple sources cited.
- Critical analysis of prior methods; clear identification of gaps.
- Demonstrates awareness of current research trends.

Meets Expectations (7–8):
- Adequate review; several sources cited.
- Basic comparison between existing methods and project approach.

Below Expectations (5–6):
- Minimal review; few sources cited.
- Superficial discussion of related work.

Unacceptable (<5):
- No literature review provided.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
III. Design and Methodology (20 points)

Criteria:
- Detailed explanation of solution approach and rationale (8 points)
- Selection and justification of data structures/algorithms used (7 points)
- Description of implementation plan or workflow (5 points)

Exceeds Expectations (18–20):
- Solution design is innovative and well-articulated.
- Choices of data structures/algorithms are justified with technical reasoning.
- Workflow is logical, detailed, and easy to follow.

Meets Expectations (14–17):
- Design addresses the problem adequately.
- Data structure/algorithm choices are explained but lack depth.
- Workflow is mostly clear.

Below Expectations (10–13):
- Design lacks detail or originality.
- Choices are poorly justified or generic.
- Workflow is incomplete.

Unacceptable (<10):
- Design not described; methodology missing.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
IV. Implementation and Technical Execution (20 points)

Criteria:
- Accuracy and completeness of code implementation (8 points)
- Effective use of chosen data structures/algorithms in code (6 points)
- Documentation and code readability (3 points)
- Evidence of testing/debugging procedures (3 points)

Exceeds Expectations (18–20):
- Code functions correctly with no major errors.
- Data structures/algorithms are implemented efficiently and appropriately.
- Well-documented code; comments explain non-trivial sections.
- Testing procedures are thorough; results included.

Meets Expectations (14–17):
- Code mostly works as intended; minor issues present.
- Use of data structures/algorithms generally appropriate.
- Code documentation present but could be improved.
- Basic testing described.

Below Expectations (10–13):
- Significant errors in code execution.
- Inefficient or incorrect use of data structures/algorithms.
- Little documentation; minimal testing evidence.

Unacceptable (<10):
- Code not included or does not run at all.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
V. Results, Analysis, and Evaluation (15 points)

Criteria:
- Presentation and interpretation of results/output (6 points)
- Comparison against benchmarks or alternative approaches where applicable (5 points)
- Discussion of strengths, limitations, and potential improvements (4 points)

Exceeds Expectations (13–15):
- Results are clearly presented using tables/figures as appropriate.
- Thoughtful analysis comparing results to benchmarks/literature.
- Limitations discussed candidly; suggestions for future work included.

Meets Expectations (10–12):
- Results presented with basic interpretation.
- Some comparison provided; limited analysis depth.
- Limitations mentioned briefly.

Below Expectations (7–9):
- Results presented without analysis or context.
- No comparison provided; limited evaluation.

Unacceptable (<7):
- No results or analysis included.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
VI. Communication, Structure, and Presentation Quality (10 points)

Criteria:
- Organization and logical flow of report sections (4 points)
- Clarity, grammar, spelling, professional language usage (3 points)
- Proper formatting: headings, figures/tables, references, appendix if needed (3 points)

Exceeds Expectations (9–10):
- Report is well-organized; transitions between sections are smooth.
- Writing is clear, concise, free from errors; tone is professional throughout.
- Formatting enhances readability; all required elements present.

Meets Expectations (7–8):
- Report structure mostly logical; minor lapses in organization.
- Writing generally clear with some errors; formatting acceptable.

Below Expectations (5–6):
- Poorly organized report; difficult to follow sections.
- Frequent grammatical/spelling errors; unprofessional tone at times.
- Formatting detracts from readability; missing elements.

Unacceptable (<5):
- Report lacks structure; writing unclear/unreadable.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
VII. Oral Presentation Preparation [Bonus up to 5 points]

Criteria:
(Note: These bonus points will be awarded after the presentation session.)
 - Prepared slides summarizing key aspects of project
 - Clear articulation during presentation
 - Ability to answer questions confidently

Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research  
Special Issue Call for Papers:  
Adversarial Machine Learning and Robust AI Systems  
Submission Deadline: November 30, 2024

**Guest Editors:**  
Dr. Laura Bennett, University of Cambridge  
Dr. Rajesh Kumar, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi  
Dr. Grace Li, Stanford University  

**Overview**

The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in real-world applications has brought about significant advancements across diverse domains such as healthcare, finance, transportation, and security. However, the growing reliance on machine learning models has also exposed critical vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks and robustness failures. Adversarial machine learning—a field focused on understanding and mitigating these vulnerabilities—has emerged as an essential area of research to ensure the safe and reliable deployment of AI technologies.

This special issue aims to bring together cutting-edge research addressing theoretical foundations, practical methodologies, and empirical studies related to adversarial machine learning and robust AI systems. We invite submissions that explore novel approaches for detecting, defending against, and understanding adversarial threats; designing inherently robust models; evaluating system-level security; and establishing benchmarks and standards for trustworthy AI.

**Topics of Interest**

We welcome original research articles, reviews, and position papers covering (but not limited to) the following topics:

- **Adversarial Attacks**
  - Generation and characterization of adversarial examples
  - Attack strategies for supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning models
  - Black-box vs. white-box attack methodologies
  - Real-world case studies of adversarial attacks on deployed systems

- **Defenses Against Adversarial Attacks**
  - Novel defense mechanisms: adversarial training, regularization techniques, certified defenses
  - Robust optimization methods
  - Detection and mitigation strategies for adversarial inputs
  - Defensive distillation and model hardening

- **Robustness Evaluation**
  - Metrics and benchmarks for robustness evaluation
  - Large-scale empirical studies on robustness across datasets and architectures
  - Explainability in robust model evaluation
  - Transferability of robustness across tasks

- **Trustworthy and Secure AI Systems**
  - Formal verification methods for machine learning models
  - Privacy-preserving machine learning in adversarial settings
  - Security implications in federated learning environments
  - System-level design for resilient AI applications

- **Theory of Adversarial Machine Learning**
  - Theoretical analysis of model vulnerabilities
  - Foundations of robustness guarantees
  - Game-theoretic perspectives on adversarial interactions

- **Applications and Case Studies**
  - Robustness in autonomous vehicles, medical diagnostics, finance, etc.
  - Deployment challenges in industry-scale AI systems
  - Human-in-the-loop solutions for robust decision-making

- **Benchmarks, Tools, and Datasets**
  - Development of open-source tools for adversarial ML research
  - New datasets for evaluating adversarial robustness
  - Community resources for standardized evaluation

Authors are invited to submit original manuscripts that have not been published or are not currently under consideration elsewhere. All submissions will undergo a rigorous peer-review process coordinated by the guest editors.

**Manuscript Preparation:**
- Manuscripts should be prepared according to the Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research (JAIR) submission guidelines: [https://www.jair.org/submission-guidelines](https://www.jair.org/submission-guidelines)
- Submissions may be up to 25 pages (excluding references), written in English.
- Supplementary materials (code, data) may be included as appendices or links.

1. Visit JAIR’s online submission portal: [https://www.jair.org/submit](https://www.jair.org/submit)
2. Select “Special Issue: Adversarial Machine Learning and Robust AI Systems” as the article type.
3. Upload your manuscript as a single PDF file.
4. Include a cover letter specifying how your work aligns with the theme of the special issue.
5. Optionally provide information regarding conflicts of interest or preferred reviewers.

**Important Dates**

- Submission Deadline: **November 30, 2024**
- First Round Reviews: January 15, 2025
- Revision Deadline: March 1, 2025
- Final Decision Notification: April 10, 2025
- Special Issue Publication: June/July 2025

*Note:* Early submissions are encouraged. Manuscripts submitted before the deadline may receive expedited review.

**Review Process**

All submissions will be evaluated by at least two independent experts in the field. The review criteria include originality, technical soundness, relevance to the special issue theme, clarity of presentation, reproducibility (where applicable), and significance of contributions.

Authors may be invited to submit revisions based on reviewer feedback. Accepted articles will be published online first before inclusion in the print edition.

**Open Access Policy**

JAIR is committed to open access publishing. All accepted articles will be freely available on the journal’s website upon publication. Authors retain copyright under a Creative Commons license.

**Special Issue Awards**

To recognize outstanding contributions:
- One Best Paper Award ($1000 USD)
- Two Honorable Mention Awards ($500 USD each)

Awarded papers will be featured prominently on the journal website and social media channels.

Dear Editorial Team,

I am finalizing the camera-ready version of our accepted paper for ICML 2025. Could you please confirm whether we should use the 2025 LaTeX template or the 2024 version still applies?

--- Email In ---

--- Attachment ---
ICML 2025 Camera-Ready Submission Template and Guidelines

Thank you for your submission to ICML 2025. This document provides detailed instructions and requirements for preparing the camera-ready version of your accepted paper using the ICML 2025 LaTeX template. Please read all guidelines carefully to ensure your paper complies with the conference standards.

I. GENERAL INSTRUCTIONS

1. Use of Template  
All camera-ready submissions must use the official ICML 2025 LaTeX template provided with this document. Do not modify the layout, font sizes, margins, or other stylistic elements of the template except as specified in these guidelines.

2. Paper Length  
Regular papers: Maximum 8 pages for main content, excluding references and appendices.  
Short papers: Maximum 4 pages for main content, excluding references and appendices.  
References may be included on additional pages beyond the main content limit. Appendices are allowed but will not be included in the proceedings; they must be uploaded separately as supplementary material.

3. File Formats  
Submit your camera-ready paper in PDF format only. Ensure that all fonts are embedded and that the file is readable on standard PDF viewers.

II. FORMAT SPECIFICATIONS

1. Page Size  
Use US Letter (8.5 x 11 inches) as the page size.

2. Margins  
Top margin: 1 inch (2.54 cm)  
Bottom margin: 1 inch (2.54 cm)  
Left margin: 0.75 inch (1.9 cm)  
Right margin: 0.75 inch (1.9 cm)

3. Font  
Main text: Times New Roman, 10-point font size  
Section headings: Times New Roman, bold, 12-point font size  
Subsection headings: Times New Roman, bold, 10-point font size  
Figures/tables captions: Times New Roman, italic, 9-point font size

4. Line Spacing  
Single-spaced throughout the document.

5. Columns  
Use two-column format throughout, except for title and author information at the top of the first page.

III. STRUCTURE OF THE PAPER

1. Title and Author Information  
Center the title at the top of the first page using boldface, Times New Roman, 16-point font size. Below the title, list all authors’ names and affiliations centered using Times New Roman, 11-point font size.

Include corresponding author’s email address below affiliations.

2. Abstract  
Provide an abstract of up to 250 words immediately following the author information, before beginning the main body of text.

3. Keywords  
List up to five keywords below the abstract to aid in indexing and searchability.

4. Main Body Sections  
Organize your paper with clear section headings such as Introduction, Related Work, Methodology, Experiments/Results, Discussion, Conclusion.

Use numbered sections (e.g., “1 Introduction”, “2 Related Work”, etc.).

IV. FIGURES AND TABLES

1. Placement and Format  
Place figures and tables within columns when possible; if necessary, they may span both columns but should be placed at the top or bottom of a page rather than in the middle.

2. Quality  
Ensure all figures are high-resolution (at least 300 dpi), legible when printed in black-and-white, and do not exceed column width unless spanning both columns.

3. Captions  
Provide concise captions below each figure or table in italicized Times New Roman, 9-point font size.

4. Referencing  
Refer to all figures and tables explicitly in the text (e.g., “see Figure 2”).

V. EQUATIONS

Display equations clearly within columns whenever possible using standard LaTeX math environments (e.g., \begin{equation}). Number equations consecutively throughout your paper (do not restart numbering per section).

VI. REFERENCES

1. Citation Style  
Use author-year citation style (e.g., Smith et al., 2023). Use BibTeX with natbib package for references.

2. Reference List  
Place reference list at end of document after main content; references can extend beyond page limit for main content.

3. Formatting Examples  

Example journal article:  
Smith J., Doe A., & Lee K., “A novel algorithm for data clustering,” Journal of Machine Learning Research, vol. 25(4), pp. 123-145, 2023.

Example conference paper:  
Brown T., Green S., “Deep learning architectures for time series analysis,” Proc. ICML, pp. 200-210, Vienna, Austria, July 2024.

VII. SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIALS AND APPENDICES

Supplementary materials such as code or additional experiments should be uploaded separately during camera-ready submission process; they will not be included in proceedings but may be made available to reviewers or readers via links.

Appendices may be included at end of PDF but will not count toward main content page limit nor appear in published proceedings.

VIII. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS AND DISCLOSURES

Acknowledgments should appear in a separate section before References.

Include funding sources and any relevant disclosures/conflicts of interest.

IX. ETHICAL COMPLIANCE STATEMENT

All accepted papers must include a statement regarding ethical compliance if applicable (e.g., use of human subjects data). Place this statement before References if needed.

X. SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS

1. Upload Process  
Log into CMT or OpenReview system using your author credentials and select your accepted paper entry under “Camera-Ready Submission”.

Upload:

- Final PDF
- Source files (.tex and figures)
- Supplementary materials (if any)

Check that all files compile correctly and display as intended prior to upload.

2. Metadata Confirmation  
Update title, author list, affiliations, abstract, and keywords as needed in submission system metadata fields; ensure these match those in your final PDF exactly.

3. Copyright Form  
Complete copyright transfer form as required by ICML; you will receive a separate email with instructions for electronic signature upon successful camera-ready upload.

XI. COMMON ISSUES AND SOLUTIONS

1. Margin Overflow / Page Limit Exceeded
Do not adjust margins or font sizes to fit more content; instead revise text to comply with limits.
Check final PDF carefully to confirm no overflow errors (“Overfull hbox” warnings).

2. Figures Not Displaying Properly
Embed all graphics using standard LaTeX commands (\includegraphics).
Avoid using external image links.
Test PDF on multiple platforms before submission.

3. Missing Fonts
Embed all fonts when generating PDF.
Avoid non-standard fonts; stick to those specified above.
If using MacOS or Linux systems, check generated PDF properties for embedded fonts before submitting.

4. Bibliography Formatting Errors
Ensure BibTeX entries are complete and accurate.
Use natbib package with appropriate options.
Check author-year citation style matches examples given above.

XII. ACCESSIBILITY GUIDELINES

To maximize accessibility:

- Avoid color-only distinctions in figures.
- Use descriptive figure captions.
- Provide alt-text for key images if possible via LaTeX packages.
- Ensure mathematical notation is clear and readable when printed or viewed electronically.
- Use plain language where possible without sacrificing technical accuracy.

XIII. POLICIES ON REVISIONS AND AUTHORSHIP CHANGES

No changes to authorship order or additions/removals will be permitted after camera-ready deadline except under exceptional circumstances subject to approval by ICML Publication Committee.

Minor edits to title or abstract may be requested prior to publication proof stage; major revisions are not permitted after acceptance notification unless approved by committee.

XIV. CONTACT INFORMATION FOR ASSISTANCE

For questions regarding formatting issues or submission process:
Email: publications@icml.cc
Subject line: “ICML 2025 Camera-Ready Inquiry – [Paper ID]”

For technical support related to LaTeX template:
Consult README.txt included with template files.
Contact technical-support@icml.cc if unresolved after checking documentation.


XV. DEADLINE FOR CAMERA-READY SUBMISSION

All camera-ready papers must be submitted by **March 15th, 2025** at **23:59 Anywhere on Earth (AoE)** time zone.


XVI. CHECKLIST FOR FINAL SUBMISSION

Before uploading your camera-ready paper:

[ ] Used official ICML 2025 LaTeX template
[ ] Complied with page limits for main content
[ ] Embedded all fonts in final PDF
[ ] Included complete author information and correct affiliations
[ ] Provided abstract and up to five keywords
[ ] Checked quality/resolution of figures/tables
[ ] Verified citations/references formatting
[ ] Included acknowledgments/disclosures if applicable
[ ] Added ethical compliance statement if applicable
[ ] Uploaded supplementary materials separately (if any)
[ ] Updated metadata in submission system to match final PDF


Thank you for your attention to these guidelines! Adherence ensures timely publication and professional presentation of your work in ICML 2025 proceedings.

- High submission volumes during peak periods

All participants in TNNLS peer review process adhere strictly to IEEE’s policies regarding confidentiality and ethical conduct.

This special issue aims to bring together cutting-edge research addressing the security challenges associated with trustworthy AI systems.

We invite original research articles, systematization of knowledge papers, and visionary perspectives that advance our understanding of how to build secure, robust, and trustworthy AI systems. Submissions should present novel contributions at the intersection of AI and security/privacy, with clear relevance to real-world applications or theoretical advancements.

Topics of Interest  
We welcome submissions covering, but not limited to, the following topics:

- **Model Poisoning Attacks and Defenses:** Techniques for attacking and defending machine learning models during training or inference phases, including federated learning scenarios.
- **Adversarial Machine Learning:** Methods for generating adversarial examples; defenses against evasion, extraction, and inversion attacks.
- **Secure Data Collection and Annotation:** Mechanisms ensuring integrity and confidentiality during data acquisition for AI models.
- **Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning:** Approaches such as differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation applied to training/inference.
- **Robustness of AI Systems:** Strategies for enhancing resilience against noisy inputs, out-of-distribution data, or malicious perturbations.
- **Explainability and Trust in AI Security:** Methods for interpreting model decisions with respect to security properties; frameworks for quantifying trustworthiness.

- **AI in Cybersecurity Applications:** Use of AI techniques for intrusion detection, malware analysis, vulnerability assessment, threat intelligence.
- **Secure Deployment of AI Models:** Secure containers/environments for deploying models; secure updates/patching mechanisms.
- **Ethical Considerations in Secure AI:** Societal impacts of insecure/untrustworthy AI; frameworks for responsible disclosure and mitigation.
- **Benchmarking and Evaluation:** Datasets, metrics, and evaluation protocols for assessing security/trustworthiness of AI systems.

============================================================
Instructions for Authors
============================================================

Thank you for choosing to submit your manuscript to the Journal of Machine Learning Systems (JMLS). This template is designed to help authors prepare manuscripts in accordance with our current formatting requirements. Please read all instructions carefully and refer to this template throughout the preparation of your submission.

This template is provided for use with Overleaf and LaTeX. It includes all required structural elements, section headings, and style guidelines.

------------------------------------------------------------
1. GENERAL GUIDELINES
------------------------------------------------------------

- Manuscripts must be written in clear, concise English.
- All submissions should be prepared using this Overleaf template.
- The main document must be compiled as a single PDF file.

- All references must conform to the journal’s citation style (see Section 9).

2. MANUSCRIPT STRUCTURE
------------------------------------------------------------

The following sections are required, in order:

1. Title Page
2. Abstract
3. Keywords
4. Introduction
5. Related Work
6. Methods
7. Results
8. Discussion
9. Conclusion
10. Acknowledgements (optional)
11. References
12. Appendices (if applicable)

Each section should begin with the corresponding heading.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. TITLE PAGE
------------------------------------------------------------

Include the following information on the title page:

- Full title of the manuscript (bold, size 16pt)
- List of authors (full names; corresponding author indicated with an asterisk)
- Affiliations (include institution name, city, country)
- Corresponding author email address
- Date of submission

Example:

---
**Deep Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Vehicle Navigation**

Fiona Zhang\textsuperscript{1,*}, Wei Li\textsuperscript{1}, Mark Chen\textsuperscript{2}

\textsuperscript{1}Department of Computer Science, Peking University, Beijing, China  
\textsuperscript{2}School of Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, USA  

*Corresponding author: fzhang@pku.edu.cn

Submitted: August 15, 2025  
---

------------------------------------------------------------
4. ABSTRACT AND KEYWORDS
------------------------------------------------------------

Abstract:
- Maximum 250 words.
- Summarize objectives, methods, results, and significance.

Keywords:
- Provide 3–6 keywords separated by commas.

Example:

---
**Abstract:**  
We present a novel deep reinforcement learning approach for autonomous vehicle navigation in urban environments...

**Keywords:** Deep learning, Reinforcement learning, Autonomous vehicles, Urban navigation
---

------------------------------------------------------------
5. SECTION HEADINGS AND SUBSECTIONS
------------------------------------------------------------

Section headings should be bold and numbered (e.g., “1 Introduction”). Subsections may be used as needed (e.g., “2.1 Model Architecture”).

All sections should follow the logical flow outlined in Section 2 above.

------------------------------------------------------------
6. FIGURES AND TABLES
------------------------------------------------------------

Figures:
- Place figures as close as possible to their first reference in text.
- Number sequentially (Figure 1, Figure 2, etc.).
- Include descriptive captions below each figure.
- Ensure all figures are referenced in the text.

Tables:
- Number sequentially (Table 1, Table 2, etc.).
- Include captions above each table.
- Use horizontal lines only at the top and bottom of tables and below column headers.

All figures and tables must be clear and legible in black-and-white print.

Example Figure:

---
\begin{figure}[ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{sample_figure.png}
\caption{Architecture of the proposed reinforcement learning model}
\label{fig:model_architecture}
\end{figure}
---

Example Table:

---
\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\hline
Method & Accuracy (\%) & F1 Score \\
\hline
Proposed & 92.4 & 0.88 \\
Baseline & 89.7 & 0.84 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\caption{Performance comparison between proposed and baseline methods}
\label{tab:performance_comparison}
\end{table}
---

------------------------------------------------------------
7. EQUATIONS AND MATHEMATICAL NOTATION
------------------------------------------------------------

Equations should be centered and numbered consecutively.

Example:

---
\begin{equation}
Q(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) \max_{a'} Q(s',a')
\label{eq:q_learning}
\end{equation}
---

All variables must be defined when first mentioned.

Use standard mathematical notation; avoid excessive use of symbols unless necessary.

------------------------------------------------------------

Journal Article:

Book:

---

Use BibTeX or manual entry as appropriate.

------------------------------------------------------------

Supplementary materials should be included as appendices at the end of the manuscript if necessary.

------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------

Subject: Question About Overleaf Template for Journal Submission

Dear Editorial Office,

I am preparing my manuscript for submission to your journal. Could you confirm whether the Overleaf template provided on your website is still valid, or has it been updated recently?

Sincerely,
Dr. Fiona Zhang
Peking University

--- Email In ---
Subject: Re: Question About Overleaf Template for Journal Submission

Dear Dr. Zhang,

Thank you for reaching out. The Overleaf template was updated in August 2025. Please use the attached version for all new submissions.

Best,
Taylor Reed
Editorial Assistant, Journal of Machine Learning Systems

--- Attachment ---
JOURNAL OF MACHINE LEARNING SYSTEMS  
Overleaf Manuscript Template  
Updated August 2025

============================================================
Instructions for Authors
============================================================

Thank you for choosing to submit your manuscript to the Journal of Machine Learning Systems (JMLS). This template is designed to help authors prepare manuscripts in accordance with our current formatting requirements. Please read all instructions carefully and refer to this template throughout the preparation of your submission.

This template is provided for use with Overleaf and LaTeX. It includes all required structural elements, section headings, and style guidelines.

------------------------------------------------------------
1. GENERAL GUIDELINES
------------------------------------------------------------

- Manuscripts must be written in clear, concise English.
- All submissions should be prepared using this Overleaf template.
- The main document must be compiled as a single PDF file.
- Figures, tables, and supplementary material should be embedded within the manuscript, not submitted as separate files.
- All references must conform to the journal’s citation style (see Section 9).
- Maximum length: Regular articles should not exceed 12 pages (excluding references and appendices); short communications are limited to 6 pages.

------------------------------------------------------------
2. MANUSCRIPT STRUCTURE
------------------------------------------------------------

The following sections are required, in order:

1. Title Page
2. Abstract
3. Keywords
4. Introduction
5. Related Work
6. Methods
7. Results
8. Discussion
9. Conclusion
10. Acknowledgements (optional)
11. References
12. Appendices (if applicable)

Each section should begin with the corresponding heading.

------------------------------------------------------------
3. TITLE PAGE
------------------------------------------------------------

Include the following information on the title page:

- Full title of the manuscript (bold, size 16pt)
- List of authors (full names; corresponding author indicated with an asterisk)
- Affiliations (include institution name, city, country)
- Corresponding author email address
- Date of submission

Example:

---
**Deep Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Vehicle Navigation**

Fiona Zhang\textsuperscript{1,*}, Wei Li\textsuperscript{1}, Mark Chen\textsuperscript{2}

\textsuperscript{1}Department of Computer Science, Peking University, Beijing, China  
\textsuperscript{2}School of Engineering, Stanford University, Stanford, USA  

*Corresponding author: fzhang@pku.edu.cn

Submitted: August 15, 2025  
---

------------------------------------------------------------
4. ABSTRACT AND KEYWORDS
------------------------------------------------------------

Abstract:
- Maximum 250 words.
- Summarize objectives, methods, results, and significance.

Keywords:
- Provide 3–6 keywords separated by commas.

Example:

---
**Abstract:**  
We present a novel deep reinforcement learning approach for autonomous vehicle navigation in urban environments...

**Keywords:** Deep learning, Reinforcement learning, Autonomous vehicles, Urban navigation
---

------------------------------------------------------------
5. SECTION HEADINGS AND SUBSECTIONS
------------------------------------------------------------

Section headings should be bold and numbered (e.g., “1 Introduction”). Subsections may be used as needed (e.g., “2.1 Model Architecture”).

All sections should follow the logical flow outlined in Section 2 above.

------------------------------------------------------------
6. FIGURES AND TABLES
------------------------------------------------------------

Figures:
- Place figures as close as possible to their first reference in text.
- Number sequentially (Figure 1, Figure 2, etc.).
- Include descriptive captions below each figure.
- Ensure all figures are referenced in the text.

Tables:
- Number sequentially (Table 1, Table 2, etc.).
- Include captions above each table.
- Use horizontal lines only at the top and bottom of tables and below column headers.

All figures and tables must be clear and legible in black-and-white print.

Example Figure:

---
\begin{figure}[ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{sample_figure.png}
\caption{Architecture of the proposed reinforcement learning model}
\label{fig:model_architecture}
\end{figure}
---

Example Table:

---
\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\hline
Method & Accuracy (\%) & F1 Score \\
\hline
Proposed & 92.4 & 0.88 \\
Baseline & 89.7 & 0.84 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\caption{Performance comparison between proposed and baseline methods}
\label{tab:performance_comparison}
\end{table}
---

------------------------------------------------------------
7. EQUATIONS AND MATHEMATICAL NOTATION
------------------------------------------------------------

Equations should be centered and numbered consecutively.

Example:

---
\begin{equation}
Q(s,a) = r(s,a) + \gamma \sum_{s'} P(s'|s,a) \max_{a'} Q(s',a')
\label{eq:q_learning}
\end{equation}
---

All variables must be defined when first mentioned.

Use standard mathematical notation; avoid excessive use of symbols unless necessary.

------------------------------------------------------------
8. CITATIONS AND REFERENCES
------------------------------------------------------------

Citations within text:
- Use numerical citations in square brackets [1], [2], etc.
- Multiple citations should be comma-separated [3,4].

Reference list:
- List references numerically in order of appearance.
- Follow this format:

Journal Article:
Author(s). Title. Journal Name Volume(Issue), pages (Year).

Conference Paper:
Author(s). Title. Proceedings of Conference Name, pages (Year).

Book:
Author(s). Title. Publisher (Year).

Example Reference List:

---
References

[1] Mnih V., Kavukcuoglu K., Silver D., et al. Human-level control through deep reinforcement learning. Nature 518(7540), 529–533 (2015).

[2] Sutton R.S., Barto A.G. Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction. MIT Press (2018).

[3] Lillicrap T.P., Hunt J.J., Pritzel A., et al. Continuous control with deep reinforcement learning. Proc NeurIPS, pp. 4297–4306 (2016).
---

Use BibTeX or manual entry as appropriate.

------------------------------------------------------------
9. SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIALS AND APPENDICES
------------------------------------------------------------

Supplementary materials should be included as appendices at the end of the manuscript if necessary.

Appendices must have clear section headings (e.g., “Appendix A: Experimental Details”).

Data or code may also be uploaded separately during submission; please indicate this in the cover letter.

------------------------------------------------------------
10. ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS AND FUNDING DISCLOSURE
------------------------------------------------------------

Acknowledgements:
Briefly acknowledge contributors who do not meet authorship criteria or funding sources.

Funding Disclosure:
List all financial support received for the research presented.

Example:

---
Acknowledgements  
We thank Dr. Ming Zhao for helpful discussions on model evaluation.

Funding  
This work was supported by NSFC Grant No. XXXX1234 and Beijing Municipal Research Fund No. ABCD5678.
---

------------------------------------------------------------
11. ETHICS STATEMENT AND DATA AVAILABILITY (IF APPLICABLE)
------------------------------------------------------------

If your work involves human subjects or sensitive data:

Ethics Statement:
Describe approval from relevant ethics committees or institutional review boards.

Data Availability:
Indicate whether datasets used in your study are publicly available or how they can be accessed upon reasonable request.

Example:

---
Ethics Statement  
All experiments involving human participants were approved by the Peking University Ethics Committee under protocol PKU2025/01.

Data Availability  
The dataset analyzed during this study is available at https://github.com/fzhang/drl-autonomous-data.
---

------------------------------------------------------------
12. AUTHOR CONTRIBUTIONS STATEMENT (OPTIONAL)
------------------------------------------------------------

State individual contributions using CRediT taxonomy if desired.

Example:

---
Author Contributions  
Conceptualization: F.Z.; Methodology: F.Z., W.L.; Software: W.L.; Validation: M.C.; Writing – original draft: F.Z.; Writing – review & editing: W.L., M.C.
---

------------------------------------------------------------
13. FORMATTING DETAILS AND STYLE REQUIREMENTS
------------------------------------------------------------

Font: Times New Roman or Computer Modern Roman  
Font Size: Main text—11pt; Section headings—bold; Title—16pt bold  
Line Spacing: Single  
Margins: Top/bottom—2cm; Left/right—2cm  
Page Numbers: Bottom center  
Color Figures: Permitted but ensure clarity in grayscale print

Do not include headers or footers other than page numbers.

Do not use footnotes except where strictly necessary; consider including explanatory text within main body instead.

Do not include watermarks or logos in figures/tables unless required for scientific interpretation.

All abbreviations must be defined upon first use.

Do not use personally identifying information except on title page and acknowledgements/funding statements as appropriate.


============================================================
LaTeX Template Structure Example
============================================================

Below is an outline showing how your Overleaf/LaTeX source file should be structured using this template:

---
\documentclass[11pt]{article}

% Packages recommended by JMLS
\usepackage{graphicx}
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage[numbers]{natbib}
\usepackage[top=2cm,bottom=2cm,left=2cm,right=2cm]{geometry}

% Begin Document
\begin{document}

% Title Page
\title{\textbf{Deep Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Vehicle Navigation}}
\author{
Fiona Zhang$^{1,*}$ \and Wei Li$^1$ \and Mark Chen$^2$\\ 
$^1$Department of Computer Science, Peking University\\ 
$^2$School of Engineering, Stanford University\\ 
*Corresponding author: fzhang@pku.edu.cn\\ 
Submitted: August 15, 2025 
}
\maketitle

% Abstract and Keywords
\begin{abstract}
We present a novel deep reinforcement learning approach...
\end{abstract}

\textbf{Keywords}: Deep learning, Reinforcement learning...

% Main Sections Start Here

\section{Introduction}

Text...

\section{Related Work}

Text...

% Continue with Methods, Results...

% Figures Example (see Section 6 above)

% Tables Example (see Section 6 above)

% Equations Example (see Section 7 above)

% Acknowledgements Example

% Funding Example

% Ethics Statement Example

% Data Availability Example

% Author Contributions Example

\bibliographystyle{plainnat}
\bibliography{references}

% Appendices Example

% End Document
\end{document}
---

============================================================
Checklist Before Submission
============================================================

Before submitting your manuscript via our online system:

[ ] Have you used the latest version of this template?  
[ ] Is your manuscript complete with all required sections?  
[ ] Are all figures/tables embedded and clearly labeled?  
[ ] Are references formatted according to journal style?  
[ ] Is your abstract within the word limit?  
[ ] Have you included funding/ethics/data availability statements if applicable?

============================================================
Contact Information for Questions Regarding Formatting:
============================================================

For questions regarding formatting requirements or technical issues with Overleaf,
please contact the Editorial Office at jmls-editorial@jmls-journal.org.


Thank you for preparing your submission according to these updated guidelines!

About NeurIPS  
The Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) is one of the premier international conferences in the areas of machine learning, computational neuroscience, and artificial intelligence. NeurIPS brings together leading researchers, practitioners, and students from academia and industry to discuss recent advances and future directions in these rapidly evolving fields. The conference features oral and poster presentations, workshops, tutorials, and invited talks from distinguished experts.

Acceptance Process  
All submissions to NeurIPS undergo a thorough review process. Each paper is evaluated for its originality, technical quality, significance, clarity of presentation, and relevance to the conference themes. Papers recommended for acceptance are further discussed by area chairs and program committee members before final decisions are made.

Your paper was selected from a large pool of submissions for its significant contribution to the understanding of robust representation learning in high-dimensional spaces. The reviewers highlighted the innovative approach to structured regularization proposed in your work, as well as its potential impact on both theoretical understanding and practical applications within the broader AI community.

Conference Participation  
Authors of accepted papers are expected to present their work during the main conference sessions. --- Attachment ---
IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing  
Open Access Fees and Waiver Policy – 2025

1. Introduction

The IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing (TDSC) is committed to facilitating the broadest possible dissemination of high-quality research in the field of dependable and secure computing. To support open science, TDSC offers authors the option to publish their accepted articles as Open Access, making them freely available to readers worldwide. This document details the current open access publication charges for 2025 and outlines policies for waivers and discounts, particularly for early-career researchers.

2. Open Access Publication Charges

For manuscripts accepted for publication under the Open Access model in IEEE TDSC, the following Article Processing Charge (APC) applies:

- Standard Open Access Fee: USD 2,195 per article

This fee covers all costs associated with peer review management, editorial processes, production, hosting, indexing, and archiving. Authors who opt for traditional subscription-based publication do not pay an APC; however, their articles are accessible only to subscribers or through institutional access.

3. What Does the Open Access Fee Include?

The APC ensures that your article is:
- Immediately accessible to all readers upon publication
- Indexed in major databases including IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, and others
- Compliant with funder mandates for open dissemination
- Provided with digital preservation and archiving services

The fee does not include charges for color figures or supplementary material; such features are included at no extra cost within the APC.

4. Payment Process

Upon acceptance of a manuscript for Open Access publication, corresponding authors will receive an invoice from IEEE Publications. Payment must be completed before final publication of the article. Accepted payment methods include credit card, bank transfer, or institutional purchase order.

Authors affiliated with institutions participating in IEEE’s Open Access Agreements may have APCs covered by their institution. Please consult your library or research office for details.

5. Waiver and Discount Policy

IEEE TDSC recognizes that APCs may present financial barriers for some authors. The journal offers a structured waiver and discount program aimed at supporting:

- Early-career researchers
- Researchers from low- and lower-middle-income countries
- Authors facing demonstrable financial hardship

All waiver applications are reviewed confidentially and impartially by the Editorial Office.

5.1 Early-Career Researcher Waivers

Definition: For the purpose of waivers, an early-career researcher is defined as someone who has received their terminal degree (PhD or equivalent) within the past five years.

Eligibility:
- The corresponding author must provide documentation of their degree conferral date.
- Only one early-career waiver per author per calendar year may be granted.

Waiver Details:
- Eligible early-career researchers may receive a partial waiver of up to 40% off the standard APC (i.e., a reduction of USD 878).
- Requests must be submitted during initial manuscript submission using the online portal.
- Waivers are contingent on availability of funds allocated annually to support this initiative.

Application Process:
a) Indicate “Early-Career Researcher Waiver Request” in your cover letter during submission.
b) Upload evidence of degree conferral date (e.g., diploma scan or official university letter).
c) The Editorial Office will confirm eligibility during initial checks; final waiver decisions communicated after peer review but before invoicing.

5.2 Country-Based Waivers

Authors whose primary affiliation is based in countries classified by the World Bank as Low-Income or Lower-Middle-Income may qualify for additional waivers:

- Full waiver (100%) for corresponding authors based in Low-Income countries.
- Partial waiver (50%) for corresponding authors based in Lower-Middle-Income countries.

Refer to the current World Bank list at https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519-world-bank-country-and-lending-groups.

Application Process:
a) Select “Country-Based Waiver Request” when submitting via the online system.
b) Provide proof of affiliation (institutional email address or letterhead).

5.3 Financial Hardship Waivers

If none of the above categories apply but you face exceptional financial hardship (e.g., unemployment, lack of research funding), you may request consideration:

- Hardship waivers are assessed individually and may cover up to 60% of the APC.
- All requests require a statement describing circumstances and any supporting documentation.

6. Additional Discounts

IEEE Members:  
Corresponding authors who are active IEEE members at time of submission are eligible for a 5% discount on APCs upon provision of membership number.

Institutional Agreements:  
Many universities and research institutes participate in Read & Publish agreements with IEEE that cover APCs wholly or partially. Check with your librarian or visit https://open.ieee.org/institutional-partners/ for information about your institution’s arrangements.

7. How to Apply for Waivers and Discounts

Waiver and discount requests must be made at initial submission via ScholarOne Manuscripts:

1) On the submission form, select applicable waiver/discount category.
2) Upload required documentation (degree certificate, proof of affiliation, etc.).
3) If eligible for multiple discounts/waivers, indicate preference; combined discounts are capped so total reductions do not exceed 100% of the fee.
4) Await confirmation from Editorial Office after peer review decision is made.

Late requests submitted after manuscript acceptance cannot be considered except under extenuating circumstances.

8. Notification Process

Decisions regarding waivers and discounts will be communicated via email after peer review is complete but prior to invoice issuance. Authors must respond within ten business days to confirm acceptance of offered terms.

9. Appeals

Authors who wish to appeal a waiver decision may contact tdsc-waiver@ieee.org within five business days of receiving notification. Appeals should include justification and any new supporting documentation not previously provided.

10. Funding Acknowledgements

Many funding agencies permit use of grant funds to pay open access fees; please check your grant terms or consult your institution’s grants office if unsure.

Authors who receive a waiver or discount must acknowledge this support in their published paper’s Funding section using wording such as:  
“This work was supported in part by an IEEE TDSC Open Access Fee Waiver.”

11. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)

Q1: Is there a separate submission fee?  
A: No submission fee is charged; fees apply only after acceptance if opting for Open Access publication.

Q2: Can I choose Open Access after my paper is accepted?  
A: Yes; you may elect Open Access at acceptance stage, though timely notification facilitates processing.

Q3: Can I combine multiple waivers?  
A: Multiple waivers can be combined up to a maximum coverage equal to the full APC amount (USD 2,195). Any excess cannot be refunded or transferred.

Q4: What happens if I am unable to pay even after a waiver?  
A: Please contact tdsc-waiver@ieee.org directly explaining your situation; exceptional cases may be considered at discretion of Editorial Office.

Q5: Does opting for Open Access affect peer review?  
A: No; all submissions undergo rigorous double-blind peer review regardless of chosen publication model.

12. Contact Information

For questions regarding fees, waivers, or application procedures:

IEEE TDSC Editorial Office  
Email: tdsc@computer.org  
Waiver Inquiries: tdsc-waiver@ieee.org  
Website: https://www.computer.org/csdl/journal/td/

13. Changes to Policy

Waiver availability and terms are subject to annual review based on funding resources and journal priorities. This policy document applies to articles accepted in calendar year 2025 only; future years may differ.

14. Summary Table – 2025 Fees & Waivers

| Category                          | Reduction (%) | Final APC Payable |
|------------------------------------|---------------|-------------------|
| Standard                          | 0%            | USD 2,195         |
| Early-Career Researcher            | Up to 40%     | USD 1,317         |
| Low-Income Country                 | 100%          | USD 0             |
| Lower-Middle-Income Country        | 50%           | USD 1,098         |
| Financial Hardship                 | Up to 60%     | USD 878           |
| IEEE Member Discount               | 5%            | USD 2,085         |

Note: Discounts/waivers can be combined up to total fee amount only; lowest payable amount is zero dollars.

15. Definitions

Early-Career Researcher – Author who obtained PhD/equivalent within last five years prior to submission.
Low-/Lower-Middle-Income Country – As classified by World Bank at time of submission.
Financial Hardship – Circumstances preventing ability to pay APC not otherwise covered above.
Corresponding Author – Individual responsible for manuscript correspondence throughout editorial process.

16. Revision History

Version: IEEE_TDSC_Open_Access_Fees_and_Waiver_Policy_2025.pdf  
Release Date: January 2024  
Effective Dates: Manuscripts accepted between Jan 1–Dec 31, 2025

Reviewer Confidentiality Form  
Journal of Cybersecurity Research

This confidentiality form is provided to reviewers invited to assess manuscripts submitted to the Journal of Cybersecurity Research (“the Journal”). It outlines the expectations and responsibilities regarding the handling of confidential information during the peer review process. By signing this form, you agree to adhere strictly to these terms throughout your engagement as a reviewer for the Journal.

1. Definitions

a. “Manuscript” refers to any unpublished work submitted to the Journal for consideration, including all associated data, supplementary materials, figures, tables, and correspondence.
b. “Confidential Information” includes all content contained within the manuscript and any communications related to its review that are not intended for public disclosure.

2. Reviewer Responsibilities

As a reviewer for the Journal, you are entrusted with confidential information pertaining to submitted manuscripts. Your responsibilities include:

a. Maintaining strict confidentiality regarding all aspects of the manuscript and related correspondence.
b. Not disclosing any details of the manuscript or its contents to any third party without explicit written permission from the Journal’s editorial office.
c. Not using information obtained through the review process for personal gain or in any manner that would constitute a conflict of interest.
d. Ensuring that your comments, recommendations, and decisions are fair, unbiased, and based solely on scientific merit.

3. Handling of Manuscripts

a. You will receive electronic copies of manuscripts and related materials for review purposes only.
b. You must store these documents securely and ensure they are not accessible to unauthorized individuals.
c. You agree not to copy, distribute, or reproduce any portion of the manuscript in any format outside the context of your formal review.
d. Upon completion of your review (or if you decline or withdraw from reviewing), you will delete or destroy all copies of manuscript files and associated correspondence from your devices and records.

4. Non-Disclosure Obligations

a. You shall not disclose any information about the manuscript under review—including its title, authorship (if known), content, results, hypotheses, methodologies, data sets, figures, or conclusions—to anyone outside the editorial staff of the Journal.
b. You may not discuss or cite unpublished material contained within the manuscript until it has been formally published by the Journal or another recognized publication venue.

5. Conflicts of Interest

a. If at any point during your review you become aware of a potential conflict of interest (including but not limited to personal relationships with authors, competing research interests, financial interests), you must notify the Journal immediately.

1. Introduction

This document outlines the formatting requirements for papers submitted to the SafeAI 2026 Workshop. All authors must use the official LaTeX template provided here to ensure consistency in appearance and adherence to workshop guidelines.

All submissions should be prepared in English, using clear, concise language appropriate for an international audience in artificial intelligence safety research.

---

2. General Formatting Instructions

- File Format: Submit your manuscript as a PDF generated from LaTeX source files.
- Template Usage: Use the supplied class file ‘safeai2026.cls’ (provided separately) or adapt from the standard article class as specified below.
- Fonts: Use Times New Roman or Latin Modern fonts throughout.
- Font Size: Main text should be 10 point.
- Line Spacing: Single-spaced throughout.
- Paragraphs: Indent paragraphs by 0.25 inches; do not add extra space between paragraphs.
- Margins: Follow margin specifications in Section 3.

---

3. Page Layout

- Paper Size: US Letter (8.5 x 11 inches).
- Top Margin: 1 inch
- Bottom Margin: 1 inch
- Left Margin: 1 inch
- Right Margin: 1 inch

Do not include page numbers, headers, or footers on any page.

Maximum Length: Papers may be up to 8 pages including figures, tables, and references. Additional supplementary material may be included as appendices (see Section 10).

---

4. Title and Author Information

Begin your paper with the title, author list, affiliations, and contact information.

Title:
- Centered at the top of the first page.
- Bold font, 16 point size.
- Capitalize only first word and proper nouns.

Authors:
- List all authors below the title, centered.
- Each author’s name followed by their affiliation(s) (italicized), city, country, and email address.

Example:

Safe Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Vehicles  
Ying Chen¹, Michael Smith²  
¹Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China (yingchen@sjtu.edu.cn)  
²University of California, Berkeley, USA (msmith@berkeley.edu)

For multiple affiliations per author, use superscript numbers after names to link to respective affiliations.

---

5. Abstract and Keywords

Abstract:
- Begin immediately after author information.
- Heading “Abstract” in bold.
- No indentation; justified text; maximum 250 words.
- Summarize motivation, methods, results, conclusions.

Keywords:
- After abstract; heading “Keywords” in bold.
- List up to five keywords separated by commas.

Example:

Abstract  
This paper presents a novel safe reinforcement learning algorithm for autonomous vehicles...

Keywords  
Safe reinforcement learning, autonomous vehicles, AI safety, risk assessment

---

6. Sectioning and Headings

Use numbered sections (e.g., 1 Introduction). Subsections are numbered accordingly (e.g., 2.1 Related Work).

Section Headings:
- Bold font; capitalize only first word and proper nouns; left-aligned.

Subsection Headings:
- Italicized; left-aligned.

Example:

1 Introduction

2 Methodology

2.1 Problem Formulation

Do not skip section numbers or leave gaps in numbering.

---

7. Figures and Tables

Figures:
- Place figures as close as possible to where they are first referenced.
- Center each figure on the page.
- Figure captions go below figures; left-aligned; use “Figure X:” format (e.g., Figure 1: Overview of our framework).
- Ensure all figures are high-resolution and readable when printed in black-and-white.

Tables:
- Center tables on the page.
- Table captions go above tables; left-aligned; use “Table X:” format (e.g., Table 2: Results comparison).
- Use consistent formatting for rows/columns.

All figures/tables must be referenced in main text (e.g., see Figure 3).

\begin{figure}[ht]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.8\linewidth]{example_fig.png}
    \caption{Figure 2: Performance of proposed method}
    \label{fig:performance}
\end{figure}

\begin{table}[ht]
    \centering
    \begin{tabular}{lcc}
        \hline
        Method & Accuracy & Safety Score \\
        \hline
        Ours & 92\% & 0.98 \\
        Baseline & 87\% & 0.85 \\
        \hline
    \end{tabular}
    \caption{Table 1: Experimental results}
    \label{tab:results}
\end{table}

---

Equations should be centered with equation numbers aligned right in parentheses.

Use LaTeX’s equation environment:

\begin{equation}
    S = \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i^2
    \label{eq:safety_score}
\end{equation}

Reference equations in text by their number (e.g., see Equation (2)).

Variables should be italicized; vectors/matrices bolded as needed.

---

Reference Style:
Follow IEEE citation style for references.

In-text citations:
Numbered consecutively in order of appearance [1], [2], etc.; multiple citations like [3],[4].

Bibliography:
List references numerically at end of paper under heading “References”. Use LaTeX ‘thebibliography’ environment or BibTeX with IEEEtran.bst style if preferred.

Examples:

In-text citation:
Recent advances have improved robustness [7].

Reference list entry:

[1] A. Smith and B. Jones, “Safety protocols for AI systems,” Proc. SafeAI Conf., pp. 15–22, Mar. 2024.

[2] Y. Chen et al., “Risk assessment models,” IEEE Trans. Neural Netw., vol. 32, no. 5, pp. 1234–1245, May 2025.

Web sources should include full URL and access date:

[3] SafeAI Workshop Website, https://safeaiworkshop.org/, accessed Jan. 20, 2026.

Sample LaTeX bibliography usage:

\bibitem{smith2024} A.~Smith and B.~Jones,
``Safety protocols for AI systems,''
\textit{Proc.\ SafeAI Conf.,} pp.~15--22, Mar.~2024.
\bibitem{chen2025} Y.~Chen et~al.,
``Risk assessment models,''
\textit{IEEE Trans.\ Neural Netw.,} vol.~32, no.~5, pp.~1234--1245, May~2025.
\end{thebibliography}

---

Supplementary content such as proofs, additional experiments or data can be included after the main reference section under an unnumbered section titled “Appendix”.

Each appendix should have its own heading (“Appendix A”, “Appendix B”, etc.).

Supplementary material must adhere to same formatting rules as main text.

If submitting separate supplementary files (allowed but optional), indicate this clearly in your submission email with filenames matching your main submission title.

---

Before submitting your manuscript to SafeAI 2026 Workshop via CMT or designated system:

□ PDF is generated from original LaTeX source files  
□ Paper length does not exceed eight pages (excluding appendices)

□ No page numbers/headers/footers appear on any page

---

Below is a skeleton structure for your main submission file (‘main.tex’):

\usepackage{graphicx}

\author{

Your introduction goes here...

Discuss previous research...

\section{Methodology}
Describe your approach...

\section{Experiments}
Report experimental setup/results...

\section{Conclusion}
Summarize findings...

\bibliographystyle{IEEEtran}
\bibliography{references}

% For direct bibliography instead of .bib file:
% \begin{thebibliography}{99}
%   ... entries ...
% \end{thebibliography}

% Appendices if needed
% \appendix
% \section*{Appendix A: Additional Proofs}

% End document
\end{document}

---

Contact Information

For template support or technical questions regarding submissions:
Email: safeai2026@safeaiworkshop.org
