A: No; posting your work on arXiv prior to or during submission does not affect eligibility for review at ACM TAI.

Q: Can I update my arXiv preprint while my paper is under review?  
A: Yes; you may update your preprint during peer review provided you notify the editorial office and ensure consistency between versions.

Q: Do I need to cite my own or others’ relevant preprints?  
A: Yes; all cited materials—including unpublished manuscripts—should be referenced appropriately in your bibliography.

Q: May I share reviewer feedback publicly via my preprint?  
A: No; reviewer reports are confidential unless explicit permission is granted by all parties involved.

Q: What version can I post after acceptance?  
A: You may post your accepted author manuscript (“post-print”) but not the final publisher-formatted PDF unless allowed by ACM’s policies.

18. Policy Review Schedule

This policy will be reviewed annually by the Editorial Board of ACM Transactions on AI. Updates will be communicated via the journal website and author guidelines.

Call for Papers  
Elsevier Information Fusion  
Special Issue on  
Distributed Intelligence Systems: Architectures, Algorithms, and Applications

Overview  
Recent advances in distributed computing, artificial intelligence, and edge technologies have enabled the realization of Distributed Intelligence Systems (DIS), wherein intelligent computation is performed collaboratively across multiple agents, devices, or platforms. Such systems promise enhanced scalability, robustness, privacy preservation, and real-time decision-making capabilities for a wide array of applications spanning autonomous vehicles, Internet of Things (IoT), smart cities, healthcare, industrial automation, and more.

The proliferation of edge devices and the rise of federated learning paradigms have further accelerated research into decentralized machine learning algorithms and resource-aware architectures. This special issue aims to bring together contributions from academia and industry addressing foundational theory, innovative methodologies, system implementations, and real-world deployments in the domain of distributed intelligence.

Scope  
We invite high-quality original research articles, review papers, and short communications on topics including but not limited to:

- Federated Learning and Distributed Machine Learning
    - Algorithms for collaborative training across edge devices
    - Privacy-preserving federated optimization
    - Communication-efficient model aggregation
    - Security threats and adversarial robustness in federated settings
    - Personalization strategies in federated learning

- Edge Intelligence Architectures
    - Design and implementation of edge-based AI frameworks
    - Resource allocation and scheduling for distributed inference
    - Heterogeneous device coordination
    - Energy-efficient distributed learning approaches

- Multi-Agent Systems and Collaborative Intelligence
    - Cooperative perception and decision-making among agents
    - Consensus mechanisms for distributed intelligence
    - Distributed reinforcement learning in dynamic environments
    - Coordination protocols for swarms and fleets

- Data Fusion Techniques in Distributed Settings
    - Sensor fusion across decentralized networks
    - Uncertainty modeling and trust management
    - Scalable data fusion algorithms for large-scale systems

- Security, Privacy, and Trust in Distributed Intelligence Systems
    - Secure communication protocols for DIS
    - Trusted execution environments for collaborative learning
    - Anomaly detection and mitigation strategies

- Real-world Applications and Case Studies
    - Autonomous vehicles: distributed perception & control
    - IoT-enabled smart city solutions
    - Healthcare diagnostics with distributed data sources
    - Industrial process monitoring using DIS frameworks

- Emerging Topics
    - Self-organizing distributed intelligence systems
    - Human-in-the-loop distributed AI architectures
    - Integration with 6G networks for ultra-low latency intelligence

Submission Guidelines  
All submissions should present significant original contributions that advance the state-of-the-art in distributed intelligence systems. Manuscripts must clearly articulate the problem addressed, relevant prior work, technical innovations introduced, experimental results (where applicable), limitations, and potential impact.

Types of contributions accepted:
- Full-length research articles (typically 6000–8000 words)
- Review/survey papers (up to 9000 words)
- Short communications/technical notes (3000–4000 words)

Manuscripts must be prepared according to the “Guide for Authors” available on the Elsevier Information Fusion journal website: https://www.journals.elsevier.com/information-fusion

Please ensure your manuscript:
- Is formatted as per journal requirements (single column preferred)
- Includes an abstract (max 250 words) summarizing main findings/contributions
- Clearly indicates relevance to the scope of this special issue in the cover letter

All submissions will undergo rigorous peer review by at least two independent experts. Review criteria include originality, technical quality, clarity of presentation, relevance to the special issue theme, reproducibility of results (for empirical works), and potential impact.

Submission Procedure  
To submit your manuscript:

1. Visit the Information Fusion online submission system at https://www.editorialmanager.com/inffus/
2. Select “VSI: Distributed Intelligence Systems” as the article type during submission.
3. Upload your manuscript files following instructions.
4. Provide a cover letter indicating submission to this special issue.
5. Suggest potential reviewers if possible.

Key Dates  
Manuscript Submission Deadline: October 15th, 2024  
First Round Decision Notification: December 20th, 2024  
Revised Manuscript Due: February 1st, 2025  
Final Acceptance Notification: March 20th, 2025  
Expected Publication Date: May 2025

Guest Editors  
Dr. Claudia Nguyen  
Department of Computer Science  
University of California, San Diego  
claudia.nguyen@ucsd.edu  

Prof. Ashok Mehra  
Indian Institute of Technology Delhi  
ashok.mehra@iitd.ac.in  

Dr. Lucia Rossi  
Politecnico di Milano  
lucia.rossi@polimi.it  

Contact Information  
For queries regarding scope or suitability of manuscripts, please contact Dr. Claudia Nguyen at claudia.nguyen@ucsd.edu.

About Elsevier Information Fusion  
Information Fusion is a leading international journal publishing research on theory and application of information fusion techniques from sensor-level to decision-level processes. The journal features original research articles that address challenges in multi-sensor data integration, signal processing, AI-driven fusion methods, distributed intelligence architectures, security/privacy concerns in fusion systems, as well as practical deployments.

Why Submit to This Special Issue?  
This special issue offers a unique opportunity to reach a multidisciplinary audience interested in cutting-edge developments across AI/ML, networking/distributed systems, embedded hardware/software design, cybersecurity, robotics/autonomous systems engineering, healthcare informatics, urban technology solutions, and more.

Authors will benefit from:

- Visibility among top researchers working at the intersection of AI and distributed systems.
- Rapid peer review turnaround times.
- Promotion through Elsevier’s global channels.
- Potential invitation for oral presentation at associated workshops/symposia.

Ethics & Open Access Policy  
Authors are expected to adhere strictly to Elsevier’s ethical standards regarding plagiarism (including self-plagiarism), duplicate publication/submission elsewhere during review process, conflicts of interest disclosure, authorship criteria transparency, and use of third-party materials/data. All accepted manuscripts will be published open access if authors opt for this route; standard publication fees may apply unless waivers are granted.

Frequently Asked Questions  

Q: Is federated learning within scope?   
A: Yes – federated learning algorithms/architectures/applications are core topics for this special issue.

Q: Are survey/review papers considered?   
A: We welcome comprehensive surveys/reviews provided they offer novel insights or synthesis relevant to distributed intelligence systems.

Q: Can I submit work previously posted as preprint?   
A: Yes; however you must disclose all prior versions/preprints during submission.

Q: What if my manuscript exceeds word limits?   
A: Please contact Dr. Nguyen before submission; exceptions may be made for highly significant works with extensive results/analysis.

Q: Are industrial case studies or deployment reports welcome?   
A: Absolutely – we strongly encourage submissions detailing practical experiences or lessons learned from real-world deployments.

Q: Will code/data sharing be required?   
A: While not mandatory for all submissions at present, authors are strongly encouraged to provide supporting code/data via public repositories wherever feasible to aid reproducibility.

**Title:**  
Robust Graph Learning Under Distribution Shifts

**Author:**  
Zeynep Kaya  
Middle East Technical University

**Abstract:**  
Graph-based learning methods have achieved remarkable success in various domains by leveraging the relational structure among data points. However, most existing approaches assume that the training and test data are drawn from the same distribution, an assumption often violated in practical scenarios due to distribution shifts. In this work, we propose a robust framework for graph learning under distribution shifts. Our approach integrates adversarial training with domain adaptation techniques to enhance model generalization on unseen target distributions. We provide theoretical analysis on the robustness of our method and demonstrate its effectiveness on benchmark datasets exhibiting significant distribution discrepancies. Experimental results show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines in node classification and link prediction tasks.

**Keywords:**  
Graph Learning; Distribution Shift; Domain Adaptation; Robustness; Adversarial Training

---

**1. Introduction**

Graphs offer a powerful abstraction for modeling relationships between entities in fields such as social networks, biology, and transportation. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have advanced the state-of-the-art in learning representations from graph-structured data. Despite their empirical success, most GNN models assume that both training and test data follow identical distributions—a condition rarely met in real-world applications due to evolving environments or sampling biases.

Distribution shift can degrade the performance of graph-based models when deployed in settings different from those seen during training. Addressing this challenge is crucial for ensuring reliable and robust graph learning in practice.

In this paper, we investigate robust graph learning under distribution shifts. Our main contributions are:

1. We identify key failure modes of current GNN models under various types of distribution shifts.
2. We introduce a novel framework combining adversarial training and domain adaptation strategies tailored for graphs.
3. We present theoretical guarantees for our approach’s robustness.
4. We validate our method on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating improved generalization across diverse domains.

---

**2. Related Work**

*Graph Neural Networks:* Recent years have witnessed rapid progress in GNN architectures such as GCNs, GraphSAGE, and GATs (Kipf & Welling, 2017; Hamilton et al., 2017; Veličković et al., 2018). These models aggregate neighborhood information but generally rely on the assumption of stationary data distributions.

*Domain Adaptation on Graphs:* Efforts to adapt models to new domains include transfer learning and domain-invariant representation learning (Pan & Yang, 2010). Some works have explored adapting graph embeddings via alignment techniques or adversarial objectives (Wang et al., 2021).

*Robustness to Distribution Shift:* Robust machine learning methods employ adversarial training, sample reweighting, or invariant risk minimization to mitigate performance drops under distributional changes (Arjovsky et al., 2019). However, few studies address robustness specifically in the context of graphs.

Our work builds upon these lines by explicitly targeting robustness to distribution shifts in graph learning.

---

**3. Problem Formulation**

Let \( G = (V, E) \) denote a graph with node set \( V \), edge set \( E \), feature matrix \( X \), and label vector \( Y \). The training data consists of labeled nodes sampled from a source distribution \( P_S \), while test nodes may come from a different target distribution \( P_T \).

Our goal is to learn a function \( f_\theta \) that maps node features and structure to labels such that performance on \( P_T \) is maximized, even when \( P_S \neq P_T \).

Types of distribution shift considered:

- **Covariate shift:** Feature distributions differ between source and target.
- **Label shift:** Label proportions change.
- **Structural shift:** Graph topology varies across domains.

---

**4. Proposed Method**

Our robust graph learning framework comprises two key components:

**4.1 Adversarial Training on Graphs**

We generate adversarial perturbations at both feature and structural levels during training to expose the model to worst-case scenarios:

- *Feature Perturbation:* For each node, we add bounded noise to its features.
- *Edge Perturbation:* Randomly add or remove edges within constraints.

The objective is:
\[
\min_\theta \max_{\delta_x, \delta_e} L(f_\theta(G + \delta_e, X + \delta_x), Y)
\]
where \( L(\cdot) \) denotes the supervised loss.

**4.2 Domain Adaptation via Representation Alignment**

We incorporate a domain discriminator network that distinguishes between source and target domain nodes based on learned representations. The encoder is trained adversarially to produce domain-invariant embeddings:

- *Encoder \( h_\phi \):* Maps input features/structure to latent space.
- *Discriminator \( D_\psi \):* Predicts domain label (source vs target).

The combined loss is:
\[
L_{total} = L_{supervised} - \lambda L_{domain}
\]
where \( L_{domain} \) penalizes distinguishability between source and target embeddings.

By aligning representations across domains while maintaining predictive power, our model generalizes better under distribution shifts.

---

**5. Theoretical Analysis**

We analyze robustness using empirical risk bounds under adversarial perturbations and domain divergence metrics.

Let \( d(P_S, P_T) \) denote the divergence between source and target distributions (e.g., Maximum Mean Discrepancy). We show that our approach minimizes an upper bound on expected target risk:

\[
R_{P_T}(f_\theta) \leq R_{P_S}(f_\theta) + d(P_S, P_T) + C
\]
where \( C \) depends on model capacity and perturbation magnitude.

Further details are provided in Supplementary Section A.

---

**6. Experiments**

We evaluate our method on three benchmark datasets:

1. **Cora-Shifted:** Synthetic covariate shift induced by random feature masking.
2. **Amazon-Products:** Real-world dataset with temporal splits causing structural changes.
3. **Citation-Full:** Label shift introduced via resampling.

Baseline models include standard GCNs, robust GNN variants (e.g., R-GCN), and recent domain adaptation methods.

*Metrics:* Node classification accuracy; F1 score; Robustness gap (difference between source and target performance).

*Implementation Details:* All models use Adam optimizer with initial learning rate 0.01; adversarial perturbations constrained by norm ball of radius 0.05; discriminator trained with gradient reversal layer.

---

**Results Table 1: Node Classification Accuracy (%)**

| Dataset         | Baseline | Robust GCN | Ours |
|-----------------|----------|------------|------|
| Cora-Shifted    | 72.5     | 75.8       | **79.3** |
| Amazon-Products | 65.1     | 68.4       | **71.7** |
| Citation-Full   | 60.2     | 62.6       | **66.8** |

Our framework consistently outperforms baselines under all types of distribution shift.

*Figure 1*: Performance curves depicting robustness gap across increasing levels of shift (see attached figures).

---

**7. Ablation Study**

We assess the individual contributions of adversarial training and domain adaptation:

- *Adversarial only:* Improves robustness against feature/edge noise but limited effect on domain mismatch.
- *Domain adaptation only:* Better transfer across domains but vulnerable to targeted perturbations.
- *Combined:* Achieves highest overall robustness.

Full ablation results presented in Table 2 (Supplementary Materials).

---

**8. Discussion**

Our findings highlight the importance of jointly addressing adversarial threats and domain discrepancy in graph learning systems deployed in dynamic environments.

Limitations include increased computational overhead due to adversarial example generation and potential instability during discriminator training.

Future work may explore scalable variants for large graphs or semi-supervised extension with limited labeled data in target domains.

---

**9. Conclusion**

We introduced a robust framework for graph learning under distribution shifts by integrating adversarial training with domain adaptation techniques. Both theoretical analysis and extensive experiments demonstrate significant improvements over existing methods regarding generalization to unseen domains.

Our approach paves the way for more reliable deployment of graph-based models in real-world scenarios where data distributions evolve over time or across contexts.

---

[4] Pan, S.J., & Yang, Q., "A Survey on Transfer Learning," IEEE TKDE 2010  
[5] Wang, X., et al., "Adversarial Domain Adaptation on Graphs," AAAI 2021  
[6] Arjovsky, M., et al., "Invariant Risk Minimization," arXiv preprint arXiv:1907.02893

Proposed Tutorial Title: Interpretable Reinforcement Learning

Brief Abstract (approx. 250 words):

Reinforcement learning (RL) has achieved remarkable success in solving complex sequential decision-making problems across domains such as robotics, healthcare, and finance. However, the interpretability of RL models remains a significant challenge that hinders their adoption in safety-critical applications. In this tutorial, I will provide a comprehensive overview of recent advances in interpretable reinforcement learning. We will discuss foundational concepts in RL and survey state-of-the-art methods designed to make RL policies and value functions more transparent, including model-based approaches, policy distillation, and attention mechanisms. The tutorial will also address evaluation metrics for interpretability, practical challenges in deploying interpretable RL systems, and real-world case studies. Attendees will gain insights into how interpretability can facilitate debugging, trustworthiness, and regulatory compliance in RL applications. The session is intended for both researchers new to RL and experienced practitioners seeking to incorporate interpretability into their workflows.

Journal of Intelligent Systems  
Special Issue: "AI for Social Good"  
Review Process Overview and Reviewer Evaluation Criteria

---

I. Introduction

This document provides a comprehensive overview of the peer review process and evaluation criteria for manuscripts submitted to the Special Issue on "AI for Social Good" in the Journal of Intelligent Systems. The goal is to ensure transparency, uphold rigorous academic standards, and support authors in understanding how their submissions will be assessed.

---

II. Review Process Timeline

The review process for this special issue consists of two distinct stages:

1. **Initial Editorial Screening (Weeks 1–2)**
   - Upon submission, all manuscripts are first evaluated by the editorial team.
   - This screening checks for thematic relevance, adherence to submission guidelines, and basic scientific merit.
   - Manuscripts that do not align with the scope or fail to meet minimum requirements may be desk-rejected at this stage.
   - Authors are notified within two weeks if their manuscript does not proceed to full peer review.

2. **Double-Blind Peer Review (Weeks 3–12)**
   - Manuscripts passing the initial screening enter a double-blind peer review process.
   - At least two independent reviewers with expertise relevant to both artificial intelligence and social good applications are assigned.
   - Reviewers remain anonymous to authors, and vice versa, throughout the process.
   - Reviewers are given four weeks to submit their evaluations; additional time may be allowed for complex papers.
   - The editorial team synthesizes reviewer comments and communicates a first-round decision (accept, minor revision, major revision, reject) within 10–12 weeks from initial submission.

3. **Revision and Final Decision (Variable Timeline)**
   - If revisions are requested, authors typically have 2–4 weeks to respond.
   - Revised manuscripts may be sent back to original reviewers or assessed by the editorial team.
   - Final decisions are communicated as soon as possible after satisfactory revisions.

---

III. Editorial Screening Criteria

The editorial team assesses each submission according to the following factors:

- **Scope Alignment:** Manuscript must clearly address AI methodologies or technologies with explicit application or impact on social good domains (e.g., healthcare, education, environment, public policy).
- **Originality:** Work must present novel ideas or approaches not previously published elsewhere.
- **Clarity:** Manuscript should be well-written, logically organized, and free of major language issues.
- **Compliance:** Adherence to journal formatting guidelines and ethical standards (e.g., proper citation, data availability statements).

Manuscripts failing any of these criteria may be rejected without external review.

---

IV. Double-Blind Peer Review Criteria

Reviewers evaluate manuscripts using a standardized rubric covering five core areas:

**1. Scientific Quality and Rigor**
   - Does the manuscript demonstrate sound methodology?
   - Are experiments or analyses appropriately designed?
   - Is there sufficient evidence supporting conclusions?

**2. Novelty and Contribution**
   - Does the work advance current knowledge in AI for social good?
   - Are new theories, models, algorithms, or applications introduced?
   - How does this work differ from previous studies?

**3. Relevance and Impact**
   - Is the research directly applicable to solving real-world problems related to social good?
   - Are potential benefits or implications clearly articulated?
   - Does the paper discuss limitations and future directions?

**4. Presentation and Clarity**
   - Is the manuscript clearly structured with logical flow?
   - Are figures, tables, and supplementary materials informative?
   - Is technical terminology adequately explained for an interdisciplinary audience?

**5. Ethical Considerations**
   - Has the study addressed responsible AI practices (e.g., fairness, accountability, transparency)?
   - Are ethical approvals obtained where necessary (e.g., human subjects research)?
   - Is there discussion of risks or unintended consequences?

Each area is scored on a scale from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent), accompanied by detailed reviewer comments.

---

V. Reviewer Recommendations

Based on their evaluation scores and narrative comments, reviewers recommend one of the following actions:

- **Accept:** Manuscript meets all criteria; ready for publication with minor or no edits.
- **Minor Revision:** Manuscript is strong but requires limited changes (clarifications, minor methodological corrections).
- **Major Revision:** Manuscript has significant merit but requires substantial changes (additional experiments, major rewriting).
- **Reject:** Manuscript fails to meet key criteria; unlikely to be suitable even after revision.

The final decision reflects consensus between reviewers and editorial judgment.

---

VI. Common Reasons for Rejection

To assist authors in preparing high-quality submissions, below are frequent reasons for rejection observed in past special issues:

- Lack of clear connection between AI techniques and social good outcomes
- Insufficient novelty compared to existing literature
- Methodological flaws or inadequate validation
- Poor writing quality impeding comprehension
- Ethical oversights or lack of responsible AI considerations
- Failure to follow journal formatting instructions

Authors are encouraged to carefully address these aspects before submitting.

---

VII. Guidelines for Revision

If revisions are requested:

1. Prepare a detailed response letter addressing each reviewer comment point-by-point.
2. Highlight changes made in the revised manuscript (using track changes or colored text).
3. Justify any suggestions you choose not to implement.
4. Ensure all ethical disclosures are complete and updated if new data/analyses were added.

Prompt attention to reviewer feedback enhances chances of acceptance.

---

VIII. Post-Acceptance Steps

Upon acceptance:

- The manuscript enters copyediting and typesetting phases.
- Authors will receive proofs for final corrections prior to publication.
- The article will be included in both online early access and print versions of the special issue.

Authors retain copyright under standard Journal of Intelligent Systems policies unless open access is selected.

---

IX. Special Issue Scope Clarification

For this special issue on "AI for Social Good," submissions should focus on topics including but not limited to:

- Machine learning applications in healthcare delivery
- AI-driven educational interventions
- Environmental monitoring using intelligent systems
- Disaster prediction and mitigation through AI analytics
- Fairness-aware algorithms for public policy decision-making
- Ethical frameworks for responsible AI deployment
- Community-engaged participatory AI research
- Explainable AI solutions addressing marginalized populations

Interdisciplinary studies bridging computer science with social sciences/humanities are especially encouraged.

---

X. Confidentiality & Conflict of Interest Policies

All submitted manuscripts are treated as confidential documents throughout review.

Reviewers must declare any conflicts of interest with assigned papers; alternative reviewers will be appointed if necessary.

Authors may suggest preferred/excluded reviewers during submission; final assignments remain at editorial discretion.

---

XI. Contact Information & Support

For questions about your manuscript status or clarification on review procedures, please contact:

Editorial Office  
Journal of Intelligent Systems  
Email: jis.editorial@intelligent-systems.org

We aim to support authors throughout the submission process and welcome feedback on our review system.

---

| Stage                    | Duration            | Outcome/Action                        |
|--------------------------|---------------------|---------------------------------------|
| Submission               | Day 0               | Author submits manuscript             |
| Editorial Screening      | Weeks 1–2           | Desk rejection or move to peer review |

| Final Decision           | Within 4 weeks      | Acceptance / Rejection                |
| Copyediting & Proofs     | Post acceptance     | Publication preparation               |
